mcqs.question: What is the role of the host in the host/device programming model?
options: The host executes the parallel kernel body directly alongside the device
The host only exists in multi-GPU systems, not single-GPU systems
The host and device are interchangeable terms for the same processor
The host allocates device memory, copies data, and launches kernels, but does not execute the parallel work itself
mcqs.explanation: The CPU (host) orchestrates — allocating, copying, and launching — while the GPU (device) executes the kernel body. Host and device are distinct processors, and the split exists even in single-GPU systems.

mcqs.question: Why are GPU threads organized into blocks rather than launched as one flat pool?
options: A block is scheduled onto physical hardware as a unit, which is what lets threads within it share fast on-chip memory and synchronize, unlike threads in different blocks
It's purely a software convention with no hardware basis
Blocks exist only to limit the maximum number of threads a program can launch
Threads in different blocks always run faster than threads in the same block
mcqs.explanation: The block boundary reflects a real hardware scheduling unit, which is exactly why intra-block cooperation (shared memory, synchronization) is possible while inter-block cooperation generally isn't. It's not just a thread-count cap, and there's no inherent speed difference tied to block membership.

mcqs.question: In the vector-add kernel example, why is there no explicit loop over the array elements in the kernel code?
options: Because the compiler automatically inserts a hidden loop over all elements
Because each of the n launched threads runs the kernel body once, using its own computed index — the 'loop' is expressed by the number of threads launched, not by iteration
Because vector addition doesn't require processing every element
Because the array size n is always known at compile time, eliminating the need for a loop
mcqs.explanation: GPU parallelism replaces explicit iteration with launching many threads, each handling one element via its computed index. There's no hidden compiler loop, every element is still processed, and n is a runtime parameter, not a compile-time constant.

mcqs.question: Why does an algorithm with strong sequential dependencies between iterations map poorly onto the standard GPU kernel model?
options: GPUs cannot execute loops of any kind
Sequential algorithms always run faster on a GPU regardless of dependencies

The map-style kernel model assumes independent, parallel invocations with no shared state carried between them — a true sequential dependency chain has to be restructured, not just ported, to fit that model
GPU kernels can only operate on floating-point data, excluding most sequential algorithms
mcqs.explanation: The kernel model's core assumption is independence across invocations; genuine cross-iteration dependencies violate that and require algorithmic restructuring. GPUs can execute loops, aren't limited to floating point, and sequential dependency chains generally hurt rather than help GPU performance.

mcqs.question: A GPU port shows a very fast kernel runtime but the overall pipeline barely got faster. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The GPU's compute throughput was measured incorrectly and is actually much slower than reported
The host-to-device and device-to-host PCIe copy time surrounding the kernel dominates the wall-clock time, even though the kernel itself is fast
PCIe transfer time is always negligible, so this must be a measurement error in the kernel itself
The kernel is not actually running on the GPU at all
mcqs.explanation: PCIe bandwidth is far lower than on-device memory bandwidth, so for kernels with little compute per byte, the copies to and from device memory can dwarf kernel execution time. Measuring only kernel runtime hides this -- real pipelines minimize the effect by keeping data resident on-device across many kernel launches instead of transferring per call.

mcqs.question: Copying 1GB to the device, running a 2ms kernel, and copying 1GB back at 25GB/s PCIe bandwidth takes about 82ms total. What does the 2.4% compute share imply for optimizing this workload?
options: Nothing can be done; this workload is fundamentally unsuited to any optimization
The kernel itself needs to be rewritten to run faster, since it is the bottleneck
PCIe bandwidth is irrelevant to this workload's total time
The real win comes from reusing device-resident data across many more kernel launches, amortizing the ~80ms copy cost over far more compute
mcqs.explanation: With copies costing 80ms against just 2ms of compute, the kernel is nowhere near the bottleneck -- the fix is batching more compute per transfer, keeping data resident on the device across many kernel launches so the fixed copy cost is amortized over much more useful work, rather than optimizing the already-fast kernel.
